prompt_c2:
You are a streetscape inventory annotator. Look ONLY at the uploaded streetscape image.
Return JSON ONLY. No markdown, no commentary, no reasoning.
 Task: record what is visible in the scene. Do not score, do not give design advice.
 Schema:
{
"road_type": "highway|arterial|neighborhood_street|alley|plaza|unclear",
"elements": {
"sidewalk": "true|false|unclear",
"bike_lane": "true|false|unclear",
"seating": "true|false|unclear",
"shade_trees": "none|few|many|unclear",
"curb_ramp": "true|false|unclear",
"tactile_paving": "true|false|unclear",
"pedestrian_crossing": "true|false|unclear",
"street_lighting": "true|false|unclear",
"greenery": "none|low|medium|high|unclear",
"vehicle_traffic": "none|light|heavy|unclear",
"bus_stop": "true|false|unclear"
},
"issues": ["no_seating", "little_shade", "no_bike_lane", "poor_accessibility", "narrow_sidewalk", "no_crossing", "high_traffic_exposure"],
"brief": "One or two English sentences describing the visible street scene."
}
 Rules:
- If an element is not clearly visible, use "unclear". Do not guess.
- "issues" may only list problems that are visible. Use [] if none.
- "brief" must mention concrete objects (sidewalk, trees, lanes, benches, ramps, etc.).

This includes not only appropriate sidewalks and places for resting but the use of parking and curb space to create more awareness and attentiveness to yielding. In terms of statements about the rights to this space, most rights statements directly touch on this as well, whether it be adequate space for pedestrians, or bicyclists. For example, Breines and Dean’s 1974 Bill of Rights include many elements within this functional area, especially when they focus on path- ways that are, “separate from trucks, buses and automobiles” (Breines & Dean, 1974). Furthermore, Levinson’s new Bill of Rights, states: “The space on a right-of-way allocated per pedestrian shall be no less than space allocated per traveler by vehicle.” He accompanies this with the hashtag “#SpatialEquity.” Human rights to the street: Ethical frameworks to guide planning, design, and engineering decisions 917 4.1.3 Calming traffic speeds and flows While speed and traffic flow are critically important to the safety and livability of our streets, it is often referenced in slightly indirect ways in these bills of rights. For example, “Cross the street calmly and safely” or “The right to cross without intimidation from motorists, whether in the crosswalk or not” both imply slower speeds and lower traffic flows. One exception is the National Street Services more direct prescription for pedestrian’s “right to lower motorists’ speed.” Finally, Donald Appleyard’s statement of people’s right to a “Street as a Safe Sanctuary” relates to all three of the above functional areas: Getting people safely across, along, and calming traffic speeds and flows (Appleyard et al., 1981). Likewise as referenced before there are many engineering strategies that have been used globally to facilitate more calm streets and related policies; from trees, to the number of windows, to appropriate modal separation to traffic flow (Ewing, Hajrasouliha, Neckerman, Purciel- Hill, & Greene, 2015). A growing body of work even discusses the advantages of two way streets for calmer traffic and a safer pedestrian experience (Riggs & Gilderbloom, 2016, 2017). 4.1.4 Livability, health, amenities & aesthetics This functional area addresses needs stated in rights related to sensory qualities of the environment, ad- dressing rights that deal with how a street should work to make people feel comfortable and secure (Los Angeles Walks, n.d.), as well as providing a healthy environment (Breines & Dean, 1974). The modernist movement and functionalism provide many examples of how architects expose the use of the ramp and the lift. One of Le Corbusier’s arguments for the Marseilles Unité d`Habitation was precisely the rapid lifts that could move people fast vertically, “You will have an elevator in motion (rising or descending) every 40 ft., that is to say, in a few seconds.” And we find the ramp used for access both for the Bauhaus building by Walter Gropius in Berlin and in Oscar Niemeyer’s buildings in Niteroi near Rio de Janeiro. the site within 2 hours and set up safety warning signs. 1.4 Paving Where the width of the roadside green belt is relatively large, it may be designed as an open green space. Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant. Figure 1.4-6 Example of paving for comprehensive roads F. Smart city demonstration roads No special requirements

      "Mature trees on both sides create a shaded, residential atmosphere that supports a pleasant everyday environment.",
      "A few people are visible talking near the entrance, suggesting some social use and neighborhood familiarity.",

      "The dense tree canopy provides substantial greenery, which supports cooling, shade, and ecological value.",

    ],
    "aesthetics": [

      "The simple low-rise buildings and walls give the street a quiet, coherent village-like character.",
      "The paved surface and edges look somewhat plain and worn, so the scene is pleasant mainly because of vegetation rather than refined streetscape materials."
    ],
    "comfort": [
      "Extensive tree shade over much of the lane improves thermal comfort in sunny weather.",
      "The road surface appears relatively even and unobstructed, which supports basic physical comfort for walking.",
      "Because there is no dedicated sidewalk and people stand close to the travel path, psychological comfort may be reduced when vehicles pass, even though the setting otherwise feels calm and uncrowded."
    ],
    "walkability": [
      "The street is narrow and likely low-speed, which can make short local walking trips feasible.",
      "There is no clearly separated sidewalk, curb-protected pedestrian zone, or marked crossing space, so walkability is limited for all road users on foot.",

    ]

prompt_c3:
As a city streetscape evaluation expert, please analyze the uploaded streetscape image based on the specified persona perspective and evaluation indicators, and return a JSON result.
 Persona Selection
Road User Type
- All Road Users
- Pedestrians
- Cyclists
- Drivers
Socially Vulnerable Groups
- All Social Groups
- Persons with Disabilities
- Adolescents (<18)
- Older Adults (≥60)
Current Selection:
All Road Users; All Social Groups
 Indicator Selection
Justice
- Equity
- Fairness
- Accessibility
Safety
Livability
Sustainability
Aesthetics
Comfort
- Thermal Comfort
- Physical Comfort
- Psychological Comfort
Walkability
Bikeability
Selected Indicators:
Justice; Safety; Livability; Sustainability; Aesthetics; Comfort; Walkability
 1. Evaluation Dimensions
Justice: Analyze whether the environment fairly distributes spatial resources, including Equity (rationality of asset distribution), Fairness (non-discriminatory rules), and Accessibility (barrier-free physical design).
Comfort: Analyze physical perception at a micro-scale, including Thermal Comfort (shade/vegetation), Physical Comfort (paving/seating), and Psychological Comfort (noise/crowding).
Core Indicators: Safety, Livability, Sustainability, Aesthetics, Walkability, and Bikeability.
 2. Persona Perspective Requirements:
The analysis must strictly adhere to the persona's characteristics. For example:
Persons with Disabilities: Focus on curb ramps, continuity of tactile paving (blind tracks), and physical obstacles.
Elderly: Focus on resting facilities, slope gradients, and summer shade.
Teenagers: Focus on traffic calming measures and social surveillance (Eyes on the street).
 3. How to use the image vs retrieved knowledge:
- The IMAGE is the primary evidence. Score only what is visible or reasonably inferable from the photo.
- Section 6 provides retrieved guidelines and research. Use them to interpret the image (what the scene should provide for this persona/indicators), not to invent objects that are not in the photo.
- If retrieved text conflicts with the image, trust the image and say so in the explanation.
- Explanations must cite specific visible objects (benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings, etc.). When a guideline is used, briefly connect it to those objects.
 4. Output Format Requirements (Return JSON ONLY, no extra text):

"Separated bike lanes reduce conflict with vehicles",

"Clear separation between sidewalk and driveway enhances walking safety"
],

"Ground-floor commercial units and visible activity indicate a vibrant environment",
"Proximity to convenience stores and community facilities meets daily needs",
"Pedestrian activity on the street increases community vitality"
],

"The presence of bike lanes and bus stops supports low-carbon travel",
"Low tree coverage indicates a lack of green infrastructure",
"No obvious rainwater infiltration facilities found"

"High street cleanliness and well-maintained environment",

],

],
"walkability": [
"Sidewalk continuity and width support safe walking",

]
}
}

1. All scores must include one decimal place.
2. Each array in explanations must contain at least 3 reasons based on specific objects in the image (e.g., benches, ramps, tree shade, lane markings).
3. Analysis content must strictly match the persona setting; generic evaluations unrelated to the specified perspective are strictly prohibited.

This is reinforced by researchers like Schlossberg and Ruiz who detail how aspects of the built environment shape pedestrian safety but also how lively and comfortable a street can be for pedestrians (Ruiz-Apilanez, Arnaiz, & de Urena, 2015; Schlossberg, Rowell, Amos, & Sanford, 2015). This includes not only appropriate sidewalks and places for resting but the use of parking and curb space to create more awareness and attentiveness to yielding. In terms of statements about the rights to this space, most rights statements directly touch on this as well, whether it be adequate space for pedestrians, or bicyclists. For example, Breines and Dean’s 1974 Bill of Rights include many elements within this functional area, especially when they focus on path- ways that are, “separate from trucks, buses and automobiles” (Breines & Dean, 1974). Furthermore, Levinson’s new Bill of Rights, states: “The space on a right-of-way allocated per pedestrian shall be no less than space allocated per traveler by vehicle.” He accompanies this with the hashtag “#SpatialEquity.” Human rights to the street: Ethical frameworks to guide planning, design, and engineering decisions 917 4.1.3 Calming traffic speeds and flows While speed and traffic flow are critically important to the safety and livability of our streets, it is often referenced in slightly indirect ways in these bills of rights. For example, “Cross the street calmly and safely” or “The right to cross without intimidation from motorists, whether in the crosswalk or not” both imply slower speeds and lower traffic flows. One exception is the National Street Services more direct prescription for pedestrian’s “right to lower motorists’ speed.” Finally, Donald Appleyard’s statement of people’s right to a “Street as a Safe Sanctuary” relates to all three of the above functional areas: Getting people safely across, along, and calming traffic speeds and flows (Appleyard et al., 1981). Likewise as referenced before there are many engineering strategies that have been used globally to facilitate more calm streets and related policies; from trees, to the number of windows, to appropriate modal separation to traffic flow (Ewing, Hajrasouliha, Neckerman, Purciel- Hill, & Greene, 2015). A growing body of work even discusses the advantages of two way streets for calmer traffic and a safer pedestrian experience (Riggs & Gilderbloom, 2016, 2017). 4.1.4 Livability, health, amenities & aesthetics This functional area addresses needs stated in rights related to sensory qualities of the environment, ad- dressing rights that deal with how a street should work to make people feel comfortable and secure (Los Angeles Walks, n.d.), as well as providing a healthy environment (Breines & Dean, 1974). This func- tional area also includes actions for placemaking and the provision of amenities for socializing, relaxing, rejuvenation (via adequate space, street furniture, vegetation, art, etc.). Along these lines, we can include building, planning, and design that provides human-scale , enclosure, memorability, transparency, etc. as discussed by Handy and Ewing in their study uncovering important urban design qualities for pedes- trians (Handy, Boarnet, Ewing, & Killingsworth, 2002). Much about Accessibility and Safety, but Little about Aesthetics and Architectural Heritage It is easy to understand the focus on accessibility and safety when working with the different juridical tools for the right for persons with some sort of impairment. Formulations such as removing manmade barriers of physical, economical and organizational character naturally have to use the accessibility views. It is easy to understand for everybody that the door must not be to narrow, that a single step in the floor or the pavement is a barrier for a person using a wheelchair. This knowledge is already implemented in standards, acts and regulations with measures of doors, turning circles for wheelchairs and design guidelines for stairs and ramps. And it is easy to register if a doorway is too narrow or a ramp too steep. And in USA at least can give you good reasons to sue someone and take them to court. More difficult with argument of aesthetics and architectural heritage. 4. Paths and paved areas in roadside green spaces shall meet the following requirements: 1. The material and thickness of the paving surface layer shall be coordinated with the road greening style and use function, and integrated with sponge city design. Ecological permeable materials should be used where possible, with anti-slip functions, and polished surface materials shall not be used. 2. Paved areas should have shading measures, and the shaded area in summer should preferably be greater than 50% of the recreational activity area. 1.4.1 Paving Style and Color 1. Quality improvement of non-motorized vehicle lane paving In riverside greenways and other leisure spaces, or at locations with a significantly high incidence of traffic accidents involving motor vehicles and non-motorized vehicles, non-motorized vehicle lanes may use colored paving. Isolation facilities may be appropriately arranged to improve the cycling experience for non-motorized vehicles. Figure 1.4-1 Schematic diagram of non-motorized vehicle lane paving 2. Quality improvement of sidewalk paving 11 A. Traffic-function roads The sides of traffic-function roads are mainly non-open interfaces, with relatively few non-traffic activities, and the paved areas mainly serve traffic distribution functions. Paving design shall implement the concepts of safety, health, comfort, and people-oriented design. Figure 1.4-2 Example of paving for traffic-function roads B. Living-service roads The activity groups on living-service roads include residents and workers around the road, as well as people from other areas who come for shopping and strolling. In terms of paving materials, color, texture, and grain, attention shall be paid to people’s perceptions, and localized creative design shall be applied to road entrances to enrich the walking experience. Figure 1.4-3 Example of paving for living-service roads C. Scenic leisure roads According to the characteristics of scenic leisure roads and the behavioral characteristics of the activity groups, the design objective of the paved area is to provide a safe, comfortable slow-traffic environment and leisure space. The paving surface layer shall use natural, aesthetically pleasing, comfortable, and ecological materials, while also meeting the requirement of coordination with the surrounding landscape. 12 Figure 1.4-4 Example of paving for scenic leisure roads D. Historic-style streets and lanes The paving design of historic-style streets and lanes shall continue and reflect cultural charm and local character, and shape distinctive spaces. Road design should focus on creating a historical and cultural atmosphere. The paving materials and texture shall be integrated with the surrounding environment. Figure 1.4-5 Example of paving for historic-style streets and lanes E. Comprehensive roads Comprehensive roads have a relatively high degree of mixing in road functions and interface types. They shall take into account the different needs of multiple characteristics, optimize the slow-traffic travel experience, consider the composite needs of road functions and the businesses on both sides, and create a paving system that is highly adaptable and simple and elegant.
